props.title: The Battle of Algiers
props.initialSlug: Colonial uprising ignites war in 1950s Algeria

sections.content: The Battle of Algiers (1966) revolutionized political filmmaking with its raw, documentary-style portrayal of the Algerian independence struggle. Director Gillo Pontecorvo created such convincing scenes of urban warfare that the Pentagon screened it in 2003 as a case study in counter-terrorism. Shot in stark black and white with handheld cameras, the film feels more like captured news footage than staged drama. This groundbreaking approach influenced later works like Z (1969) and Missing (1982), establishing a new grammar for politically urgent cinema.

sections.content: The film's influence extends deep into modern political cinema. Munich (2005) borrowed its tense urban warfare sequences, while The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006) echoed its unflinching look at revolutionary violence. Pontecorvo's genius was refusing to moralize - he shows both French paratroopers and FLN fighters as trapped in a cycle of escalating violence, each believing in their cause's righteousness.

Ennio Morricone's score deserves special attention, mixing traditional Algerian music with modernist orchestration to create mounting tension. This innovative soundtrack approach influenced countless political thrillers, from The Day of the Jackal (1973) to Syriana (2005). The film's use of non-professional actors, including real FLN members, created an authenticity that still feels revolutionary today. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern War Cinema

sections.content: Contemporary war films like Zero Dark Thirty (2012) and Green Zone (2010) clearly draw from Pontecorvo's techniques. His approach to staging large crowd scenes - mixing documentary footage with carefully choreographed chaos - became a template for depicting urban unrest. Children of Men (2006) director Alfonso Cuarón specifically cited The Battle of Algiers as inspiration for his long-take street battle sequences.
